3:103.ar: وَٱعۡتَصِمُواْ بِحَبۡلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعࣰ ا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُواْۚ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِذۡ كُنتُمۡ أَعۡدَآءࣰ فَأَلَّفَ بَيۡنَ قُلُوبِكُمۡ فَأَصۡبَحۡتُم بِنِعۡمَتِهِۦٓ إِخۡوَٰنࣰ ا وَكُنتُمۡ عَلَىٰ شَفَا حُفۡرَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱلنَّارِ فَأَنقَذَكُم مِّنۡهَاۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُونَ
3:103.en: And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the edge of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided

3:105.ar: وَلَا تَكُونُواْ كَٱلَّذِينَ تَفَرَّقُواْ وَٱخۡتَلَفُواْ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا جَآءَهُمُ ٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتُۚ وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمۡ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمࣱ‏
3:105.en: And do not be like the ones who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment

SuWirnjanys.speaker: adnan
SuWirnjanys.speaker_note: continues his own Ramadan values series, mentions growing up in Saudi Arabia and Syria and London
SuWirnjanys.title: The Values of Islam: Brotherhood and Unity (Ukhuwwah and Jama'ah)
SuWirnjanys.one_line: Brotherhood is the bond and unity is the structure it builds; without both, Muslims are a crowd that fragments and falls.
SuWirnjanys.summary: Closing the run of social values in his Ramadan series, he pairs brotherhood and unity as two values that cannot work apart. Brotherhood is like the bond between molecules and unity the stable structure that results; brotherhood without unity produces purposeless friendships, and unity without brotherhood becomes authoritarian conformity. He argues Muslims in the West are a crowd rather than a community unless they centralize something, and of the four options (political, social, religious, financial) only pooling zakat and endowments is realistic. He grounds the value in the Quran's statement that believers are brothers, the one-body hadith and the Prophet's pairing of Muhajirun and Ansar in Madinah, which he calls one of the miracles of prophethood. He separates healthy scholarly disagreement from destructive factionalism, insisting on unity rather than uniformity, and mocks the group-within-a-group habit that makes people belong to a faction instead of Islam. Masajid must welcome everyone as hosts in Allah's house, and congregational prayer and dua show that even the most intimate worship is done together. He ends with the fall of Muslim Spain as the lesson of petty fragmentation and asks Muslims to get over themselves and work with one another.

outline.heading: Opening
Social values versus personal values
outline.gist: He has covered values that shape relations between people and will turn to personal ones next; today's two values are deeply interdependent.

outline.heading: Brotherhood as bond, unity as structure
outline.gist: Brotherhood is the molecular bond and jama'ah the stable structure it forms, built from two people up to the whole ummah.

outline.heading: Losing one ruins the other
outline.gist: Brotherhood without unity gives purposeless friendships; unity without brotherhood gives authoritarian conformity.

outline.heading: A family versus a crowd
outline.gist: What turns a group of people into a community is the moral and emotional bond and the cohesion that lets it channel its energy.

outline.heading: Centralizing politics: not available in the West
outline.gist: Many jama'ah hadith assume a political imam, so in the West they must be read figuratively because Muslims cannot have that structure.

outline.heading: Centralizing socially: Muslims live scattered
outline.gist: Unlike Little Italy or Chinatown, Muslims here do not cluster, which he counts as a positive trait of blending in and working with everyone.

outline.heading: Centralizing religiously: still a dream
outline.gist: Unified religious leadership is the ideal but he does not believe it is achievable now.

outline.heading: Centralizing finances: the one real option
outline.gist: Pooling zakat and endowments is the only realistic way to turn Muslims here into a community rather than a crowd.

outline.heading: Believers are brothers: a fact, not a preference
outline.gist: The Quran states brotherhood as an ethical fact, and the Prophet described believers as one body and forbade enmity, desertion and oppression.

outline.heading: Looking down on a brother, and Allah uniting hearts
outline.gist: Contempt for a fellow Muslim is enough evil for a lifetime; Allah, not money, joined the believers' hearts.

outline.heading: The Madinah brotherhood as a miracle
outline.gist: Pairing Muhajirun with Ansar in shared homes, sometimes for a decade, was unheard of among Arabs and is one of the miracles of prophethood.

outline.heading: Your team, for better or worse
outline.gist: Like a child placed on a soccer team, you do not choose your fellow Muslims; you build the bond so the team works.

outline.heading: Unity, not uniformity
outline.gist: Scholarly disagreement is built into Islam and he defends opinions he rejects; the evil is factionalism that destroys cooperation.

outline.heading: Quran and hadith against division
outline.gist: Allah repeatedly commands holding together and warns against splitting like earlier peoples; the Prophet's hadith on the jama'ah are emphatic and even harsh.

outline.heading: The group-within-a-group phenomenon
outline.gist: Saying the shahadah is enough to belong; sub-groups that duplicate everything and claim to have it all figured out fragment the ummah, as he saw growing up.

outline.heading: Masajid as Allah's house: welcome everyone
outline.gist: Those serving the masjid are hosts on Allah's behalf and must welcome every visitor without checklists, as they would guests in their own home.

outline.heading: Congregational salah and dua
outline.gist: Even prayer, the most intimate act, is done in straight equal rows regardless of wealth, age or colour, and dua is made together.

outline.heading: Concentrated energy and a global ummah
outline.gist: A cohesive ummah multiplies its impact, and Muslims everywhere praying for each other is a bond that transcends race, nation and wealth.

outline.heading: Shaytan's aim: fragmentation
outline.gist: Every split halves strength; history repeatedly shows egocentric Muslim factions falling one after another.

outline.heading: The fall of Al-Andalus
outline.gist: Nearly a millennium of civilization and knowledge was lost through petty, egoistic division, down to the language itself.

outline.heading: Holding on when there is no jama'ah
outline.gist: The hadith of clinging to the root of a tree shows that without unity Muslims become sitting ducks, as events overseas show today.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: Brotherhood is an ethical fact among believers, modelled by the Madinah pairing, and must be built even with people you did not choose.

themes.label: Unity of the ummah
themes.note: Unity is not uniformity; scholarly difference is healthy but factionalism and sub-group loyalty destroy cooperation.

themes.label: Community building, cooperation and the ummah
themes.note: Muslims in the West are a crowd until they centralize something, and finances are the only realistic option.

themes.label: The masjid: its role and etiquette
themes.note: Masajid exist to keep the jama'ah and must welcome everyone as guests of Allah.

themes.label: Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance
themes.note: Congregational prayer and its equal rows embody the jama'ah even in the most intimate worship.

themes.label: Islamic history and civilization
themes.note: Al-Andalus fell through petty fragmentation and lost everything it built.

themes.label: Shaytan: his methods and how to resist him
themes.note: Fragmenting Muslims is one of Shaytan's main goals because division makes them weak.

themes.label: Muslim identity and life in the West / Canada
themes.note: Muslims in the West lack political or social centralization and blend in, which is positive but leaves them scattered.

quran.point: Believers are brothers, stated as an ethical fact rather than an invitation
Allah supported the Prophet with the believers and united their hearts, which no wealth could do
Hold fast together and do not divide
Do not be like those who split after clear proofs came to them

hadith.gist: Believers in their mutual love and mercy are like one body; when one part aches the whole body responds
Do not hate, envy or turn your backs on one another; be, servants of Allah, brothers. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim, he does not oppress or forsake him
It is enough evil for a person to look down on his Muslim brother
Stick to the jama'ah, for Shaytan is with the one alone and further from two; whoever wants the best of Paradise should keep to the jama'ah

Hudhayfah asked what to do if there is no jama'ah or imam; leave all factions even if you must bite on the root of a tree until death
Prayer in congregation is many times better than praying alone

Unity, not uniformity
Without centralizing something, you have a crowd, not a community
Believers are brothers is an ethical fact, not a preference
Destructive factionalism, not disagreement, is the problem

Little Italy and Chinatown as examples of social clustering
Fragmentation of Muslims overseas today
takeaways: Treat fellow Muslims as your team and build bonds even with those you do not like
Defend the right of others to hold scholarly opinions you disagree with
Do not let a sub-group become your identity in place of Islam

qIW9_QwdA1s.title: The Values of Islam: Rahmah (Compassion) and Rifq (Tenderness)
qIW9_QwdA1s.one_line: Rahmah is a universal human right and the bare minimum of how a Muslim treats anyone, even enemies and tyrants; rifq is how it is applied.
qIW9_QwdA1s.summary: The sheikh calls rahmah the value most associated with the Prophet, who was not only described with mercy but described as mercy itself. Hadith students traditionally begin with the narration that the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Rooted in the word for womb, rahmah means providing a safe space for growth and acknowledging human fragility, and rifq, tenderness, is its practice: you cannot hammer glass and wonder why it shatters. Borrowing from medical testing, he calls rahmah a highly sensitive test of Islam: its absence proves Islam is absent, and if learning makes you harsher, your teacher is teaching something else. Rahmah is a human right with no exceptions; punishments exist out of mercy to the collective, but even the condemned keep their dignity. He laments that torture marks many Muslim countries that perfect ritual while losing ethics, and contrasts the testimony of released Palestinian and Israeli prisoners. Prophetic examples include the sheep that must not see the blade and the bird whose eggs were returned. Rahmah allows firmness, as with parents who set consequences, but without rifq firmness becomes domination and trauma. An ethic that is not universal is only a preference: you need not love your enemy, but you can always show him mercy.

outline.heading: A value that is also an ethic

outline.heading: Rooted in the womb

outline.heading: Acknowledging fragility
outline.gist: Compassion understands people can break, which is where rifq comes in; Allah is gentle and loves gentleness.

outline.heading: Tenderness beautifies everything
outline.gist: Rifq improves whatever it enters; you cannot hammer glass and wonder why it shatters.

outline.heading: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim
outline.gist: The Prophet saw people's weakness; Allah is best known by two names from this root.

outline.heading: A highly sensitive test of being Muslim
outline.gist: Like a medical test, if rahmah is absent, Islam is absent, though its presence does not prove Islam.

outline.heading: If learning makes you harsher
outline.gist: Growing in knowledge while shrinking in empathy means you are being taught something other than Islam.

outline.heading: Rahmah is a human right

outline.heading: Punishment as mercy to the collective

outline.heading: Cells where you are treated like dirt
outline.gist: Torture has become the mark of Middle Eastern states, because ethics were lost.

outline.heading: Ritual without ethics
outline.gist: Countries that perfect prayer lines but abandon ethics have missed the point.

outline.heading: Fiqh differs, ethics do not
outline.gist: People fight over juristic details that allow difference while the unchanging ethics are non-negotiable.

outline.heading: Do not kill the sheep twice
outline.gist: The Prophet rebuked a man sharpening his knife in front of the animal he was dragging.

outline.heading: The mother bird's eggs
outline.gist: During a campaign he had a young man return the eggs he took from a nest.

outline.heading: Mercy even in war
outline.gist: He never hated his enemies, accepted their repentance and forbade harming trees, children, women, homes and worshippers.

outline.heading: Mercy can mean strictness
outline.gist: A merciful parent denies a child endless TV and ice cream; without rahmah comes domination, without rifq trauma.

outline.heading: Consequences at home
outline.gist: Truth and authority applied with tenderness form children morally, and a consequence at home is cheaper than one outside.

outline.heading: Rahmah is not weakness
outline.gist: It stands its ground and may apply strict punishment when the community needs it.

outline.heading: Dignity in custody
outline.gist: Incarceration can be dignified or brutal; Muslims held human dignity as a right a thousand years before the UN.

outline.heading: How we lost it
outline.gist: Not only governments but peoples now speak of enemies without mercy.

outline.heading: Two sets of released prisoners
outline.gist: Compare the trauma of released Palestinian prisoners with the accounts of returned Israeli captives.

outline.heading: Everyone or no one
outline.gist: You may not decide who is an exception to a right.

outline.heading: Even the tyrant
outline.gist: Tried and executed, but with mercy, because it defines us; Jahannam is Allah's justice, not our job.

outline.heading: A non-universal ethic is a preference
outline.gist: If mercy does not apply to everyone, it is only a convenience.

outline.heading: Not love thy enemy, but mercy
outline.gist: You cannot love someone trying to destroy you, but you can show him mercy, even in a bitter divorce.

outline.heading: When every other ethic fails
outline.gist: Love, respect and more can fail, but compassion can always be brought; rifq is the spice of life.

A0rM9YPtLQk.speaker: adnan
A0rM9YPtLQk.speaker_note: MWN Friday khutbah on 15 Ramadan; speaks of 'this masjid' and addresses his own congregation; no other speaker named
A0rM9YPtLQk.title: Third Week of Ramadan: Showing Commitment to Change
A0rM9YPtLQk.one_line: Mid-Ramadan: solidify the changes of the first two weeks into lifelong habits, expect tests, and learn from the Sahabah whose first Ramadan was Badr.
A0rM9YPtLQk.summary: He opens with 9:105, act and Allah, His Messenger and the believers will see your deeds, then turns to the news: eight countries bombed in days, the lands that produced Islam's early scholars being destroyed. He avoids politics, since three hundred people hold three thousand opinions, but insists on dua for the people of Sham, Iraq, Lebanon, Yemen, the Gulf, Iran and Sudan, argues that any Muslim unity would have stopped the tyrants, and tells Muslims in the West to use the seat at the table they have. Ramadan is a time-out for looking inward, and the Quran starts with the individual: you cannot predict geopolitics, but you control what you intend, do and stand for. Two weeks of fasting and night prayer already show an impressive change; now it must be solidified into lifelong, not Ramadanic, habits, guarded from the distraction of wealth and family, built on small consistent deeds. Commitment will be tested, as 29:10 warns, and Ramadan gives four weeks to build that capacity. The Sahabah's first Ramadan brought Badr: called to reclaim their stolen goods they argued they no longer needed the money, but it was about standing for truth, since there is no dignity in surrendering what was taken from you. Outnumbered, the first army in Arabia bound by moral glue rather than blood won the day that separated truth from falsehood. He asks everyone to keep their new habits for months and report back.

outline.heading: Opening
Act, and Allah will see your deeds
outline.gist: 9:105: live your life and do what you will, for Allah, His Messenger and the believers witness it, and you will be returned to your Lord to be held to account.

outline.heading: The birthplace of the deen under bombardment
outline.gist: Every quiet period ends in more death in the region where Islam was born. Islam reached every continent because of the early scholars of Sham, Iraq, Iran and Arabia who taught, documented and protected it, and every part of that land is being destroyed; eight countries bombed in a few days.

outline.heading: Not politics, but the people
outline.gist: He stays out of the region's politics, where three hundred people hold three thousand opinions driven by emotion, and focuses on what all agree on: the wellbeing of people who lived their whole lives under regimes that cared nothing for their rights.

outline.heading: Make dua for them
outline.gist: Every colour in the room came from that land, and if life there were good no one would have left. Make dua for the people of Sham, Iraq, Lebanon, Yemen, the Gulf, Iran and Sudan, who were barely making ends meet before the bombs.

outline.heading: Unity stops tyrants, and a voice at the table
outline.gist: Any Muslim unity on any front would have prevented this; powers that cannot let a decade pass without war itch to bomb brown people. Muslims in the West must also advocate, because they can sit at the table where others cannot.

outline.heading: Ramadan is a time-out
outline.gist: No better time for this message than Ramadan, when you step back, look inward and ask what you are doing with your life and whether you live it meaningfully for Allah.

outline.heading: The Quran starts with the individual
outline.gist: You cannot predict international politics, but you can control what you feel, intend, think and do: your participation, your contribution and where you stand.

outline.heading: Two weeks of impressive change
outline.gist: Two full weeks of fasting every day and praying every night speak to your character; anyone observing you would see a person less distracted, more focused and devoted than before Ramadan.

outline.heading: Do not let wealth and family distract you
outline.gist: Now solidify the commitment. 63:9: wealth and children, the two closest blessings you rightly thank Allah for, must never distract you from remembering Him and why He created you.

outline.heading: Small consistent deeds
outline.gist: When you change, know what you are moving towards and what you leave behind. The most beloved deeds to Allah are the consistent ones, even small, simple ones no one will thank you for; that is how change begins.

outline.heading: Lifelong habits, not Ramadanic habits
outline.gist: No one can fast and pray every night after Ramadan, but pick the positive changes you want to hold on to as a way of showing Allah your commitment, and plan them as habits that define who you are.

outline.heading: Commitment will be tested
outline.gist: 29:10: some claim commitment until they are harmed for Allah's sake, then treat people's trial as worse than Allah's punishment and step back. Real change always meets obstacles that test how much pushback you will take; Allah will not let us off the hook that easily, and Ramadan comes four weeks in a row to build that capacity.

outline.heading: The Sahabah's first Ramadan
outline.gist: On a day like this, 1445 lunar years ago, Ramadan was defined to them for the first time: the doors of heaven opened, the doors of Jahannam closed, the devils removed, a night better than a lifetime. A little perseverance for an amazing deal.

outline.heading: The 17th: a call to reclaim the stolen caravan
outline.gist: Ramadan with the Prophet, who often prayed at home to keep things easy for them. On the morning of the 17th he called them out to intercept the caravan Abu Sufyan was leading with the wealth Quraysh had confiscated from them for their belief.

outline.heading: Reluctance before Badr (8:5-7)
outline.gist: After two years in Madinah they had wealth and argued they would give up their stolen property for Allah's sake, when deep down they did not want to provoke Quraysh. 8:5-7: your Lord brought you out in truth while a party of believers were averse, arguing as if driven to death, wishing for the unarmed caravan.

outline.heading: Refuse oppression however it is packaged
outline.gist: It was about righteousness, not money. A Muslim stands up against transgression whatever mask it wears. Take back what is rightfully yours, then gift it if you wish; surrendering what was taken by force is neither courage, generosity nor dignity.

outline.heading: Makkah held on, Madinah had to embody
outline.gist: For thirteen years in Makkah they were told not to bear arms and only had to persevere and hold on to the deen. In Madinah, with a country, holding on was no longer enough: they had to carry Islam's values everywhere.

outline.heading: Righteousness has to be demonstrated
outline.gist: Islam stands for the truth at all times, beyond dispute; the Quran exposed their reluctance because the truth had to be shown. It was a frightening day: 313 or 314 men with the Prophet, and scholars differ on the number.

outline.heading: The caravan escapes, Quraysh marches
outline.gist: Abu Sufyan anticipated them and took another route. At Badr the caravan was gone and Quraysh marched with a thousand men and more cavalry than the entire Muslim army, which had two horsemen and little training or arms.

outline.heading: An army of moral glue
outline.gist: Facing the undefeated champion of the region, for the first time in Arabia an army stood together not on tribe, blood, vengeance or raiding but on a shared cause: a Qurashi beside an Ansari beside a man from the Roman Empire.

outline.heading: The day truth and falsehood separated
outline.gist: They fought bravely; the best of the companions are the people of Badr and the best of the angels those who helped them. After that day it was clear who stood on which side, beginning the chain of events that fills this masjid.

outline.heading: Interlude
Second khutbah: prove your commitment
outline.gist: Ramadan is the chance to show Allah the commitment to change, as the Sahabah did in their first Ramadan when sent, unprepared, outnumbered and uncertain, against the strongest power in the region; they proved it, and every good thing in the deen followed.

outline.heading: Keep it for a few months, then report back
outline.gist: Turn small changes into daily habits: a little fasting, more dhikr, night prayer, daily learning about Allah. Hold on to them for a few months after Ramadan, then come and tell him how your life, mind and commitment have changed.

outline.heading: Outro

96:3.en: Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous

96:5.en: Taught man that which he knew not

2:170.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُواْ بَلۡ نَتَّبِعُ مَآ أَلۡفَيۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَنَآۚ أَوَلَوۡ كَانَ ءَابَآؤُهُمۡ لَا يَعۡقِلُونَ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا يَهۡتَدُونَ
2:170.en: And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has revealed," they say, "Rather, we will follow that which we found our fathers doing." Even though their fathers understood nothing, nor were they guided

62:5.ar: مَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ حُمِّلُواْ ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةَ ثُمَّ لَمۡ يَحۡمِلُوهَا كَمَثَلِ ٱلۡحِمَارِ يَحۡمِلُ أَسۡفَارَۢاۚ بِئۡسَ مَثَلُ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:5.en: The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books]. Wretched is the example of the people who deny the signs of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

2:31.ar: وَعَلَّمَ ءَادَمَ ٱلۡأَسۡمَآءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ فَقَالَ أَنۢبِـُٔونِي بِأَسۡمَآءِ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
2:31.en: And He taught Adam the names - all of them. Then He showed them to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful

2:32.ar: قَالُواْ سُبۡحَٰنَكَ لَا عِلۡمَ لَنَآ إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمۡتَنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
2:32.en: They said, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, it is You who is the Knowing, the Wise

2:33.ar: قَالَ يَٰٓـَٔادَمُ أَنۢبِئۡهُم بِأَسۡمَآئِهِمۡۖ فَلَمَّآ أَنۢبَأَهُم بِأَسۡمَآئِهِمۡ قَالَ أَلَمۡ أَقُل لَّكُمۡ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ غَيۡبَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَأَعۡلَمُ مَا تُبۡدُونَ وَمَا كُنتُمۡ تَكۡتُمُونَ
2:33.en: He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names." And when he had informed them of their names, He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen [aspects] of the heavens and the earth? And I know what you reveal and what you have concealed

3:7.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أَنزَلَ عَلَيۡكَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ مِنۡهُ ءَايَٰتࣱ مُّحۡكَمَٰتٌ هُنَّ أُمُّ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ وَأُخَرُ مُتَشَٰبِهَٰتࣱۖ فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمۡ زَيۡغࣱ فَيَتَّبِعُونَ مَا تَشَٰبَهَ مِنۡهُ ٱبۡتِغَآءَ ٱلۡفِتۡنَةِ وَٱبۡتِغَآءَ تَأۡوِيلِهِۦۖ وَمَا يَعۡلَمُ تَأۡوِيلَهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُۗ وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ فِي ٱلۡعِلۡمِ يَقُولُونَ ءَامَنَّا بِهِۦ كُلࣱّ مِّنۡ عِندِ رَبِّنَاۗ وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إِلَّآ أُوْلُواْ ٱلۡأَلۡبَٰبِ
3:7.en: It is He who has sent down to you, [O Muhammad], the Book; in it are verses [that are] precise - they are the foundation of the Book - and others unspecific. As for those in whose hearts is deviation [from truth], they will follow that of it which is unspecific, seeking discord and seeking an interpretation [suitable to them]. And no one knows its [true] interpretation except Allah. But those firm in knowledge say, "We believe in it. All [of it] is from our Lord." And no one will be reminded except those of understanding

16:43.ar: وَمَآ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مِن قَبۡلِكَ إِلَّا رِجَالࣰ ا نُّوحِيٓ إِلَيۡهِمۡۖ فَسۡـَٔلُوٓاْ أَهۡلَ ٱلذِّكۡرِ إِن كُنتُمۡ لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
16:43.en: And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed [Our message]. So ask the people of the message if you do not know

2:30.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّي جَاعِلࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ خَلِيفَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَجۡعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفۡسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسۡفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ وَنَحۡنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمۡدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَۖ قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
2:30.en: And [mention, O Muhammad], when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we declare Your praise and sanctify You?" Allah said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know

35:27.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ أَنزَلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءࣰ فَأَخۡرَجۡنَا بِهِۦ ثَمَرَٰتࣲ مُّخۡتَلِفًا أَلۡوَٰنُهَاۚ وَمِنَ ٱلۡجِبَالِ جُدَدُۢ بِيضࣱ وَحُمۡرࣱ مُّخۡتَلِفٌ أَلۡوَٰنُهَا وَغَرَابِيبُ سُودࣱ‏
35:27.en: Do you not see that Allah sends down rain from the sky, and We produce thereby fruits of varying colors? And in the mountains are tracts, white and red of varying shades and [some] extremely black

33:67.ar: وَقَالُواْ رَبَّنَآ إِنَّآ أَطَعۡنَا سَادَتَنَا وَكُبَرَآءَنَا فَأَضَلُّونَا ٱلسَّبِيلَا۠
33:67.en: And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our masters and our dignitaries, and they led us astray from the [right] way

Sll_uk2HOyU.speaker: adnan
Sll_uk2HOyU.speaker_note: continues his own Ramadan values series and refers to his own sessions and circles
Sll_uk2HOyU.title: The Values of Islam: Intellect and Seeking Knowledge ('Aql and Talab al-'Ilm)
Sll_uk2HOyU.one_line: Critical thinking is a value and lifelong learning its principle; Islam treats both as worship and forbids surrendering your mind to anyone.
Sll_uk2HOyU.summary: Opening the personal values in his Ramadan series, he reframes intellect and knowledge seeking as critical thinking and lifelong learning. Intellect is the condition of religious responsibility and the only way to grasp revelation, while ignorance is the root evil, which is why the pre-Islamic era was named after it and the first revealed command was an open-ended iqra', a word meaning to gather, reflect and learn from others, not merely to read. Knowledge without thinking produces blind followers, and thinking without knowledge is limited; Islam demands both and treats learning as a moral and spiritual pursuit rather than an academic one. He uses Adam being taught the names to show that articulation and connected thought are what make humans unique. Islam had no war between religion and science; its golden age was when jurists were also scientists, and scholars who never leave the masjid lose touch with people's lives. Those in power dislike critical thinkers and prefer people knowing just enough to keep the system running. He insists one reaches certainty in Allah through questioning, then submits out of earned trust, and must never hand one's mind to parents, groups or a sheikh. He invites his own students to object and question.

outline.heading: Opening
Turning to personal values: critical thinking and lifelong learning
outline.gist: After the social values, he begins personal ones, framing intellect as critical thinking and knowledge seeking as lifelong learning.

outline.heading: Knowledge as a moral and spiritual pursuit
outline.gist: Intellect is how revelation is understood, and Islam treats learning as worship aimed at transforming perspective, not accumulating data.

outline.heading: Intellect as the condition of responsibility
outline.gist: Without a functioning mind there is no religious accountability; the word 'aql itself means to restrain and bind, as in tying the camel.

outline.heading: Ignorance as the root evil
outline.gist: The pre-Islamic era is named for the dominance of ignorance, and the Prophet brought its opposite, beginning with the command to read.

outline.heading: Iqra' without an object
outline.gist: The first verses command reading without saying what to read; iqra' means gathering, reflecting and learning from those before you, much as English uses reading figuratively.

outline.heading: Neither blind following nor unaided thinking
outline.gist: Knowledge without critical thinking makes people follow their forefathers blindly, and thinking without knowledge leaves them limited.

outline.heading: The virtue of seeking knowledge
outline.gist: After the image of a donkey carrying books, he lists hadith on the obligation and reward of seeking knowledge and explains that the prophets left knowledge, not wealth.

outline.heading: Adam taught the names: the gift of articulation
outline.gist: The first thing Allah did for humans was teach them to name and describe things, and Islam makes critical thinking an obligation one is accountable for.

outline.heading: No one followed without evidence
outline.gist: Even the Prophet brought evidence, the scholarly ethic is 'bring your proof', and all agree that ignorance is evil; the epistemology debate is left for another series.

outline.heading: Ignorance spoils whatever it touches
outline.gist: Wealth, power or youth combined with ignorance only produce greater evil; the Quran sends people to those firmly grounded in knowledge.

outline.heading: The angels and Adam's speech
outline.gist: The angels voiced their fears, admitted they knew only what they were taught, and submitted when Adam connected the names into meaningful speech.

outline.heading: The scholar-scientists of the golden age
outline.gist: Islam had no religion-versus-science struggle; it peaked when jurists were also physicians and astronomers, since revelation and creation share one source.

outline.heading: Those who truly revere Allah
outline.gist: The verse on scholars revering Allah sits among verses spanning many natural sciences, showing whom it means.

outline.heading: Why power dislikes critical thinkers
outline.gist: Governments prefer people with just enough knowledge to run the system and enough distraction not to question it; Islam obligates questioning.

outline.heading: Communal obligations of worldly knowledge
outline.gist: Not everyone must be an engineer or physician, but enough must be, and every university step is rewarded when seen as a religious pursuit.

outline.heading: Scholars confined to the masjid lose relevance
outline.gist: The early imams were merchants and professionals, which is why their jurisprudence addressed real lives.

outline.heading: Critical thinking protects the deen
outline.gist: Without it, a trusted teacher can say anything; one questions everything to reach Allah, then submits out of trust built by reason.

outline.heading: Give up your mind for no one
outline.gist: No parent, friend, boss or group deserves your freedom of thought, and followers are not excused on Judgment Day for having just followed.

outline.heading: Teachers inform, students decide
outline.gist: His role is to share information and reasons, not to control; he encourages objection in his circles because the ummah needs thinkers, not sheep.

outline.heading: How knowledge transformed the first Muslims
outline.gist: The Prophet turned an ignorant people into a nation that sanctified knowledge and saw critical thinking as an obligation.

themes.label: Seeking knowledge, learning and scholars
themes.note: Knowledge seeking is worship and transformation of perspective; ignorance is the root evil.

themes.label: Critical thinking and the use of intellect
themes.note: One must never surrender one's mind; certainty in Allah is reached through questioning and submission rests on reasoned trust.

themes.label: Methodology: how to read texts, tafsir method, intellectual approach
themes.note: The scholarly ethic is to follow the stronger evidence, and even the Prophet explained his reasons.

themes.label: Islamic history and civilization
themes.note: The golden age was when religious scholars were also scientists, with no conflict between revelation and science.

themes.label: Leadership, governance and institutions
themes.note: Those in power prefer an informed-enough but unquestioning population.

themes.label: Stories of earlier prophets
themes.note: Adam's teaching of the names and the angels' submission show what makes humans unique.

quran.point: Only those with knowledge truly revere Allah; knowledge means transformation, not data
The first revelation commands reading twice without naming an object
Those who followed what they found their forefathers doing, knowledge without critical thought
A donkey carrying books: information without understanding
Allah taught Adam the names and the angels conceded they knew only what they were taught
Those firmly grounded in knowledge are the ones to turn to
Ask the people of knowledge if you do not know
The angels' concern about corruption and bloodshed and Allah's reply that He knows what they do not
The verse on revering scholars follows descriptions of plants, mountains, people and animals
Followers who say they only obeyed their leaders are not excused

hadith.gist: A man asked whether to tie his camel or trust Allah; tie it and trust
Seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim
Whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah eases for him a path to Paradise
Angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge, even fish in the sea seek forgiveness for him, and the prophets left knowledge rather than wealth as inheritance

maxims: Knowledge seeking is a moral and spiritual pursuit, not an academic one
Intellect is the engine; knowledge is fuel and upgrade
Nothing mixed with ignorance turns into good
Give up your mind for no one
We don't need more sheep; we need thinkers
Question everything to reach Allah, then trust Him

stories.point: Adam's ability to connect names into speech is what made the angels submit; articulation and thought define humanity.

stories.who: Early imams such as Abu Hanifah, Malik and Ahmad
stories.point: They lived full lives outside the masjid, so their jurisprudence fit people's real lives.

contemporary: Governments educating people only enough to keep the economy running, while distracting them with sports and entertainment
People joining political groups or schools of thought to avoid thinking for themselves
takeaways: Treat study, including university, as worship and a lifelong pursuit
Question what you are told and ask for evidence, including from religious teachers
Seek knowledge rather than relying only on your own reasoning
Do not hand your thinking over to any group, parent or leader
Ask those firmly grounded in knowledge when you do not know

36:45.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّقُواْ مَا بَيۡنَ أَيۡدِيكُمۡ وَمَا خَلۡفَكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تُرۡحَمُونَ
36:45.en: But when it is said to them, "Beware of what is before you and what is behind you; perhaps you will receive mercy

36:46.ar: وَمَا تَأۡتِيهِم مِّنۡ ءَايَةࣲ مِّنۡ ءَايَٰتِ رَبِّهِمۡ إِلَّا كَانُواْ عَنۡهَا مُعۡرِضِينَ
36:46.en: And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they are from it turning away

36:47.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمۡ أَنفِقُواْ مِمَّا رَزَقَكُمُ ٱللَّهُ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ أَنُطۡعِمُ مَن لَّوۡ يَشَآءُ ٱللَّهُ أَطۡعَمَهُۥٓ إِنۡ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
36:47.en: And when it is said to them, "Spend from that which Allah has provided for you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Should we feed one whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed? You are not but in clear error

36:48.ar: وَيَقُولُونَ مَتَىٰ هَٰذَا ٱلۡوَعۡدُ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
36:48.en: And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful

36:49.ar: مَا يَنظُرُونَ إِلَّا صَيۡحَةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰ تَأۡخُذُهُمۡ وَهُمۡ يَخِصِّمُونَ
36:49.en: They do not await except one blast which will seize them while they are disputing

36:50.ar: فَلَا يَسۡتَطِيعُونَ تَوۡصِيَةࣰ وَلَآ إِلَىٰٓ أَهۡلِهِمۡ يَرۡجِعُونَ
36:50.en: And they will not be able [to give] any instruction, nor to their people can they return

36:51.ar: وَنُفِخَ فِي ٱلصُّورِ فَإِذَا هُم مِّنَ ٱلۡأَجۡدَاثِ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمۡ يَنسِلُونَ
36:51.en: And the Horn will be blown; and at once from the graves to their Lord they will hasten

36:52.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰوَيۡلَنَا مَنۢ بَعَثَنَا مِن مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜۗ هَٰذَا مَا وَعَدَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ وَصَدَقَ ٱلۡمُرۡسَلُونَ
36:52.en: They will say, "O woe to us! Who has raised us up from our sleeping place?" [The reply will be], "This is what the Most Merciful had promised, and the messengers told the truth

36:53.ar: إِن كَانَتۡ إِلَّا صَيۡحَةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰ فَإِذَا هُمۡ جَمِيعࣱ لَّدَيۡنَا مُحۡضَرُونَ
36:53.en: It will not be but one blast, and at once they are all brought present before Us

36:54.ar: فَٱلۡيَوۡمَ لَا تُظۡلَمُ نَفۡسࣱ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا تُجۡزَوۡنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
36:54.en: So today no soul will be wronged at all, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do

103:3.ar: إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوۡاْ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوۡاْ بِٱلصَّبۡرِ
103:3.en: Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience

68:17.ar: إِنَّا بَلَوۡنَٰهُمۡ كَمَا بَلَوۡنَآ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡجَنَّةِ إِذۡ أَقۡسَمُواْ لَيَصۡرِمُنَّهَا مُصۡبِحِينَ
68:17.en: Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden, when they swore to cut its fruit in the [early] morning

68:19.ar: فَطَافَ عَلَيۡهَا طَآئِفࣱ مِّن رَّبِّكَ وَهُمۡ نَآئِمُونَ
68:19.en: So there came upon the garden an affliction from your Lord while they were asleep

68:20.en: And it became as though reaped

7:187.ar: يَسۡـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلسَّاعَةِ أَيَّانَ مُرۡسَىٰهَاۖ قُلۡ إِنَّمَا عِلۡمُهَا عِندَ رَبِّيۖ لَا يُجَلِّيهَا لِوَقۡتِهَآ إِلَّا هُوَۚ ثَقُلَتۡ فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ لَا تَأۡتِيكُمۡ إِلَّا بَغۡتَةࣰۗ يَسۡـَٔلُونَكَ كَأَنَّكَ حَفِيٌّ عَنۡهَاۖ قُلۡ إِنَّمَا عِلۡمُهَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
7:187.en: They ask you, [O Muhammad], about the Hour: when is its arrival? Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal its time except Him. It lays heavily upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except unexpectedly." They ask you as if you are familiar with it. Say, "Its knowledge is only with Allah, but most of the people do not know

h11cbEZ9VWw.speaker: adnan
h11cbEZ9VWw.speaker_note: continues his own Yasin series; speaks of his oncology clinic and growing up in Syria
h11cbEZ9VWw.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 5 (45-54)
h11cbEZ9VWw.one_line: The opposite of a living heart: refusing to learn from past and future, refusing to give, and asking when the Hour comes instead of preparing.
h11cbEZ9VWw.summary: He returns to the surah's theme that obedience to Allah gives life its quality, since we spend far more time dead than alive and the young companions are still remembered. After showing how a heart comes alive, the verses now show its opposite through two refusals. First, when told to beware of what lies before and behind them, people turn away: they will not learn from history, their own past or others' mistakes, the frustration every parent feels when a child repeats their error. From his oncology clinic he describes how people face death according to how they lived, since religion held as mere culture does not help them then, and he urges an honest yearly audit in Ramadan. Second, told to spend, they ask why they should feed someone Allah could have fed. He calls a life without the joy of giving no life at all: inequality exists so that people can give life to others, we are only trustees of what we hold, and the owners of the burnt garden learned this. From his own Syrian past he admits how easily the comfortable ignore the suffering of others. Finally, asking when the promise will come is the wrong question; the Prophet asked what you have prepared. He describes the sudden blast, the resurrection and a judgment where no soul is wronged.

outline.heading: Submission as the source of true life
outline.gist: Yasin looks at submission from the inside: taking the deen into your heart is what makes you truly alive.

outline.heading: Quality of life and the believer's legacy
outline.gist: The Quran defines the piece of quality of life medicine misses: purpose; the young believer of the township lived better than most.

outline.heading: We spend more time dead than alive
outline.gist: Against billions of years, a lifetime barely counts, so the Quran never cares about quantity, only how you lived.

outline.heading: Companions who died young are still remembered
outline.gist: The Prophet, shown a beautiful garment, said the handkerchiefs of a companion who had died years earlier were finer in paradise.

outline.heading: From how to gain life to its opposite
outline.gist: Having shown that iman comes from observing life, the universe and history, Allah now gives two examples of the opposite.

outline.heading: Beware of what is before you and behind you
outline.gist: The disbelievers are told to be mindful; the phrase refers to the future and the past.

outline.heading: Learning from your own past and from earlier nations
outline.gist: Whether read as their own lives or the history of nations, the point is reflecting so as not to repeat harm.

outline.heading: Why parents get upset when children repeat their mistakes
outline.gist: Life is too short to walk a path someone already found worthless; that is what makes parents angry.

outline.heading: So that you may receive mercy: the ego that will not learn
outline.gist: Reflection raises the quality of life, but our sense of being unique stops us from learning from others.

outline.heading: By time: advising one another
outline.gist: Surat al-Asr: we win back time by advising each other about what is worth living and dying for.

outline.heading: The omitted answer: they turn away
outline.gist: Arabic drops what context makes obvious; the sentence is completed by the next verse's turning away.

outline.heading: Every sign ignored: facing death in the clinic
outline.gist: Seeing others die with regret is a sign; in his oncology clinic people face mortality abruptly and react according to how they lived.

outline.heading: Religion as culture does not help at death
outline.gist: When the deen was only a cultural extra, it does not kick in when death comes; what comes out is the sum of how you lived.

outline.heading: Audit your year in Ramadan; it will not just click later
outline.gist: Ask whether last year is worth repeating; graduating, marrying or a new job will not change the essence of your life.

outline.heading: Shall we feed those Allah could have fed?
outline.gist: Told to spend from whatever Allah gave them, wealth, knowledge or time, they argue Allah could feed the poor Himself.

outline.heading: A life without the joy of giving is not worth living
outline.gist: A life centred on consuming is not real life; real life includes the joy of bringing a smile to someone in need.

outline.heading: Unequal hands so we can give each other life
outline.gist: People are dealt different hands so that those who have can find life by sustaining, teaching and protecting others.

outline.heading: Consumerism romanticized
outline.gist: Individual consumption has never been so glorified, perhaps like the spoiled nations Allah punished.

outline.heading: You are only entrusted with it
outline.gist: Land outlives all its owners; the question is whether you give on your own terms before it is taken.

outline.heading: The owners of the garden
outline.gist: Sons of a generous father planned to harvest secretly to avoid the poor, and Allah burnt the garden to the ground.

outline.heading: It is easy to say not my problem when you are fine
outline.gist: The comfortable ignore the oppressed and would feel very differently in their place.

outline.heading: His Syrian experience of indifference
outline.gist: Comfortable Syrians ignored their suffering neighbours, then expected the world to care once they were under fire.

outline.heading: He loves me, look what He gave me: figurative death
outline.gist: Reading wealth as proof of Allah's love and poverty as His choice is being alive without living.

outline.heading: Reading notes: merged letters and the pause
outline.gist: He explains the merged letters in yakhissimun and the brief pause marked in verse 52 that keeps the meaning from running together.

outline.heading: When is this promise? The wrong question
outline.gist: The Prophet answered a man asking when the Hour is with what have you prepared for it; only Allah knows its time.

outline.heading: One blast while they dispute
outline.gist: All they await is a single cry that takes them in the middle of their quarrels over the world.

outline.heading: The Hour strikes in the middle of ordinary life
outline.gist: A man repairing his basin, a morsel that never reaches the mouth, a garment spread between two who never finish the sale.

outline.heading: No will, no return to their families
outline.gist: No time to say goodbye, make amends or tell loved ones they love them.

outline.heading: Only Allah remains
outline.gist: The angel of death takes the last lives and his own; existence is a fragile moment and it was always only Allah.

outline.heading: The second blast: drawn out like threads from a tangle
outline.gist: People are pulled from their graves in perfect order, each body and fingerprint restored, each nation in its place.

outline.heading: Who raised us from our sleeping place?
outline.gist: The first blast ends all existence, like dreamless sleep; those not expecting a second chapter are shocked, and all are brought together.

outline.heading: No soul will be wronged
outline.gist: Each will be judged fairly by the hand they were dealt, their circumstances and their choices.

outline.heading: Not when, but are you ready?
outline.gist: None of it will be your choice when it comes, so prepare now for the life that continues.

themes.label: Purpose, meaning and the point of life
themes.note: Quality, not length, defines a life; the young companions still live through their legacy.

themes.label: Self-honesty and self-accountability (muhasabah)
themes.note: Reflect on your own past and others' mistakes instead of assuming you are unique.

themes.label: Mortality, death and preparing for it
themes.note: People face death according to how they lived; audit your life every Ramadan.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Parents' anger at children repeating their mistakes comes from knowing how short life is.

themes.label: Zakat, charity and giving
themes.note: A life without the joy of giving is not worth living; we are trustees, as the owners of the garden learned.

themes.label: Selfishness, greed of the soul (shuhh) and selflessness
themes.note: The comfortable ignore the oppressed; his own Syrian community did the same.

themes.label: Syria
themes.note: Syrians' past indifference to suffering neighbours, then the reversal.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: The blasts of the horn, resurrection and fair judgment; ask what you have prepared, not when.

quran.point: Humanity is in loss except those who advise one another; learning from others wins back time.
The owners of the garden who planned to deny the poor and found it burnt.
Knowledge of the Hour is with Allah alone and it comes suddenly.

hadith.gist: Shown a fine garment sent as a gift by a king, the Prophet said a deceased companion's handkerchiefs in paradise are better than it (the narration concerns Sa'd ibn Mu'adh).
A man asked when the Hour is; the Prophet replied, what have you prepared for it?
The Hour will come while a man is repairing his basin, another lifting a morsel to his mouth, and two men spreading a garment they will never finish trading.
After the first blast only a few remain; the angel of death is commanded to take their lives and finally his own.

maxims: We're just dead people who haven't died yet
Allah is never interested in quantity
A life without the joy of giving isn't worth living
You're not the owner, you're entrusted
Not when it happens, but are you ready

stories.who: Patients receiving an incurable diagnosis in his clinic
stories.point: People meet death with calm or shock depending on how they lived, not on religion held as culture.
Withholding from the poor what a generous father gave brings ruin.

stories.who: Syrians before and after the war
stories.point: The comfortable ignore others' oppression until they suffer it themselves.

stories.who: The Bedouin asking about the Hour
stories.point: Ask what you have prepared, not when it will come.

contemporary: Oncology care and median-survival conversations
Consumerism and romanticized individual consumption
Palestine under occupation and Iraqi refugees in Syria
Dictatorship and people without passports or freedom of movement
takeaways: Learn from your own past and other people's mistakes instead of repeating them.
Use Ramadan each year to ask honestly whether your last year is worth repeating.
Find joy in giving wealth, time and knowledge, knowing you are only a trustee.
Do not ignore the oppressed just because you are comfortable.
Prepare for the Hour rather than asking when it will be.

18:65.ar: فَوَجَدَا عَبۡدࣰ ا مِّنۡ عِبَادِنَآ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ رَحۡمَةࣰ مِّنۡ عِندِنَا وَعَلَّمۡنَٰهُ مِن لَّدُنَّا عِلۡمࣰ ا
18:65.en: And they found a servant from among Our servants to whom we had given mercy from us and had taught him from Us a [certain] knowledge

18:66.ar: قَالَ لَهُۥ مُوسَىٰ هَلۡ أَتَّبِعُكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُعَلِّمَنِ مِمَّا عُلِّمۡتَ رُشۡدࣰ ا
18:66.en: Moses said to him, "May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement

18:67.ar: قَالَ إِنَّكَ لَن تَسۡتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبۡرࣰ ا
18:67.en: He said, "Indeed, with me you will never be able to have patience

18:68.ar: وَكَيۡفَ تَصۡبِرُ عَلَىٰ مَا لَمۡ تُحِطۡ بِهِۦ خُبۡرࣰ ا
18:68.en: And how can you have patience for what you do not encompass in knowledge

18:69.ar: قَالَ سَتَجِدُنِيٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ صَابِرࣰ ا وَلَآ أَعۡصِي لَكَ أَمۡرࣰ ا
18:69.en: [Moses] said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in [any] order

18:70.ar: قَالَ فَإِنِ ٱتَّبَعۡتَنِي فَلَا تَسۡـَٔلۡنِي عَن شَيۡءٍ حَتَّىٰٓ أُحۡدِثَ لَكَ مِنۡهُ ذِكۡرࣰ ا
18:70.en: He said, "Then if you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I make to you about it mention

18:71.ar: فَٱنطَلَقَا حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا رَكِبَا فِي ٱلسَّفِينَةِ خَرَقَهَاۖ قَالَ أَخَرَقۡتَهَا لِتُغۡرِقَ أَهۡلَهَا لَقَدۡ جِئۡتَ شَيۡـًٔا إِمۡرࣰ ا
18:71.en: So they set out, until when they had embarked on the ship, al-Khidh r tore it open. [Moses] said, "Have you torn it open to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing

18:72.ar: قَالَ أَلَمۡ أَقُلۡ إِنَّكَ لَن تَسۡتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبۡرࣰ ا
18:72.en: [Al-Khidh r] said, "Did I not say that with me you would never be able to have patience

18:73.ar: قَالَ لَا تُؤَاخِذۡنِي بِمَا نَسِيتُ وَلَا تُرۡهِقۡنِي مِنۡ أَمۡرِي عُسۡرࣰ ا
18:73.en: [Moses] said, "Do not blame me for what I forgot and do not cover me in my matter with difficulty

18:74.ar: فَٱنطَلَقَا حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا لَقِيَا غُلَٰمࣰ ا فَقَتَلَهُۥ قَالَ أَقَتَلۡتَ نَفۡسࣰ ا زَكِيَّةَۢ بِغَيۡرِ نَفۡسࣲ لَّقَدۡ جِئۡتَ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا نُّكۡرࣰ ا
18:74.en: So they set out, until when they met a boy, al-Khidh r killed him. [Moses] said, "Have you killed a pure soul for other than [having killed] a soul? You have certainly done a deplorable thing

18:75.ar: ۞قَالَ أَلَمۡ أَقُل لَّكَ إِنَّكَ لَن تَسۡتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبۡرࣰ ا
18:75.en: [Al-Khidh r] said, "Did I not tell you that with me you would never be able to have patience

18:76.ar: قَالَ إِن سَأَلۡتُكَ عَن شَيۡءِۭ بَعۡدَهَا فَلَا تُصَٰحِبۡنِيۖ قَدۡ بَلَغۡتَ مِن لَّدُنِّي عُذۡرࣰ ا
18:76.en: [Moses] said, "If I should ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion. You have obtained from me an excuse

18:77.ar: فَٱنطَلَقَا حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَآ أَتَيَآ أَهۡلَ قَرۡيَةٍ ٱسۡتَطۡعَمَآ أَهۡلَهَا فَأَبَوۡاْ أَن يُضَيِّفُوهُمَا فَوَجَدَا فِيهَا جِدَارࣰ ا يُرِيدُ أَن يَنقَضَّ فَأَقَامَهُۥۖ قَالَ لَوۡ شِئۡتَ لَتَّخَذۡتَ عَلَيۡهِ أَجۡرࣰ ا
18:77.en: So they set out, until when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to offer them hospitality. And they found therein a wall about to collapse, so al-Khidh r restored it. [Moses] said, "If you wished, you could have taken for it a payment

18:78.ar: قَالَ هَٰذَا فِرَاقُ بَيۡنِي وَبَيۡنِكَۚ سَأُنَبِّئُكَ بِتَأۡوِيلِ مَا لَمۡ تَسۡتَطِع عَّلَيۡهِ صَبۡرًا
18:78.en: [Al-Khidh r] said, "This is parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience

18:79.ar: أَمَّا ٱلسَّفِينَةُ فَكَانَتۡ لِمَسَٰكِينَ يَعۡمَلُونَ فِي ٱلۡبَحۡرِ فَأَرَدتُّ أَنۡ أَعِيبَهَا وَكَانَ وَرَآءَهُم مَّلِكࣱ يَأۡخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصۡبࣰ ا
18:79.en: As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working at sea. So I intended to cause defect in it as there was after them a king who seized every [good] ship by force

18:80.ar: وَأَمَّا ٱلۡغُلَٰمُ فَكَانَ أَبَوَاهُ مُؤۡمِنَيۡنِ فَخَشِينَآ أَن يُرۡهِقَهُمَا طُغۡيَٰنࣰ ا وَكُفۡرࣰ ا
18:80.en: And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would overburden them by transgression and disbelief

18:81.ar: فَأَرَدۡنَآ أَن يُبۡدِلَهُمَا رَبُّهُمَا خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّنۡهُ زَكَوٰةࣰ وَأَقۡرَبَ رُحۡمࣰ ا
18:81.en: So we intended that their Lord should substitute for them one better than him in purity and nearer to mercy

18:82.ar: وَأَمَّا ٱلۡجِدَارُ فَكَانَ لِغُلَٰمَيۡنِ يَتِيمَيۡنِ فِي ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ وَكَانَ تَحۡتَهُۥ كَنزࣱ لَّهُمَا وَكَانَ أَبُوهُمَا صَٰلِحࣰ ا فَأَرَادَ رَبُّكَ أَن يَبۡلُغَآ أَشُدَّهُمَا وَيَسۡتَخۡرِجَا كَنزَهُمَا رَحۡمَةࣰ مِّن رَّبِّكَۚ وَمَا فَعَلۡتُهُۥ عَنۡ أَمۡرِيۚ ذَٰلِكَ تَأۡوِيلُ مَا لَمۡ تَسۡطِع عَّلَيۡهِ صَبۡرࣰ ا
18:82.en: And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and there was beneath it a treasure for them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they reach maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. And I did it not of my own accord. That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience

19:42.ar: إِذۡ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ يَٰٓأَبَتِ لِمَ تَعۡبُدُ مَا لَا يَسۡمَعُ وَلَا يُبۡصِرُ وَلَا يُغۡنِي عَنكَ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا
19:42.en: [Mention] when he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and will not benefit you at all

19:43.ar: يَٰٓأَبَتِ إِنِّي قَدۡ جَآءَنِي مِنَ ٱلۡعِلۡمِ مَا لَمۡ يَأۡتِكَ فَٱتَّبِعۡنِيٓ أَهۡدِكَ صِرَٰطࣰ ا سَوِيࣰّ ا
19:43.en: O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to an even path

19:44.ar: يَٰٓأَبَتِ لَا تَعۡبُدِ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنَۖ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنَ كَانَ لِلرَّحۡمَٰنِ عَصِيࣰّ ا
19:44.en: O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed Satan has ever been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient

19:45.ar: يَٰٓأَبَتِ إِنِّيٓ أَخَافُ أَن يَمَسَّكَ عَذَابࣱ مِّنَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ فَتَكُونَ لِلشَّيۡطَٰنِ وَلِيࣰّ ا
19:45.en: O my father, indeed I fear that there will touch you a punishment from the Most Merciful so you would be to Satan a companion [in Hellfire]

19:46.ar: قَالَ أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنۡ ءَالِهَتِي يَٰٓإِبۡرَٰهِيمُۖ لَئِن لَّمۡ تَنتَهِ لَأَرۡجُمَنَّكَۖ وَٱهۡجُرۡنِي مَلِيࣰّ ا
19:46.en: [His father] said, "Have you no desire for my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so avoid me a prolonged time

19:47.ar: قَالَ سَلَٰمٌ عَلَيۡكَۖ سَأَسۡتَغۡفِرُ لَكَ رَبِّيٓۖ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ بِي حَفِيࣰّ ا
19:47.en: [Abraham] said, "Peace will be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord. Indeed, He is ever gracious to me

20:43.en: Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed

20:44.ar: فَقُولَا لَهُۥ قَوۡلࣰ ا لَّيِّنࣰ ا لَّعَلَّهُۥ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوۡ يَخۡشَىٰ
20:44.en: And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah]

4:94.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا ضَرَبۡتُمۡ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَتَبَيَّنُواْ وَلَا تَقُولُواْ لِمَنۡ أَلۡقَىٰٓ إِلَيۡكُمُ ٱلسَّلَٰمَ لَسۡتَ مُؤۡمِنࣰ ا تَبۡتَغُونَ عَرَضَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا فَعِندَ ٱللَّهِ مَغَانِمُ كَثِيرَةࣱۚ كَذَٰلِكَ كُنتُم مِّن قَبۡلُ فَمَنَّ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣰ ا
4:94.en: O you who have believed, when you go forth [to fight] in the cause of Allah, investigate; and do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace "You are not a believer," aspiring for the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are many acquisitions. You [yourselves] were like that before; then Allah conferred His favor upon you, so investigate. Indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted

9:114.ar: وَمَا كَانَ ٱسۡتِغۡفَارُ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ لِأَبِيهِ إِلَّا عَن مَّوۡعِدَةࣲ وَعَدَهَآ إِيَّاهُ فَلَمَّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُۥٓ أَنَّهُۥ عَدُوࣱّ لِّلَّهِ تَبَرَّأَ مِنۡهُۚ إِنَّ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ لَأَوَّٰهٌ حَلِيمࣱ‏
9:114.en: And the request of forgiveness of Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became apparent to Abraham that his father was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed was Abraham compassionate and patient

17:23.ar: ۞وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعۡبُدُوٓاْ إِلَّآ إِيَّاهُ وَبِٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ إِحۡسَٰنًاۚ إِمَّا يَبۡلُغَنَّ عِندَكَ ٱلۡكِبَرَ أَحَدُهُمَآ أَوۡ كِلَاهُمَا فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَآ أُفࣲّ وَلَا تَنۡهَرۡهُمَا وَقُل لَّهُمَا قَوۡلࣰ ا كَرِيمࣰ ا
17:23.en: And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and to parents, good treatment. Whether one or both of them reach old age [while] with you, say not to them [so much as], "uff," and do not repel them but speak to them a noble word

79:24.en: And said, "I am your most exalted lord

HIEPYw5pIKY.speaker: adnan
HIEPYw5pIKY.speaker_note: Sh. Adnan's Ramadan halqa series; recalls his village teacher in Syria and the greeting team at Muslim Wellness Network
HIEPYw5pIKY.title: Soft Speech (Ramadan 2026, Night 15: Quranic Themes 2)
HIEPYw5pIKY.one_line: Why the Quran calls for soft speech, shown through al-Khidr with Musa, Ibrahim with his father, and Musa and Harun sent gently to Pharaoh.
HIEPYw5pIKY.summary: Soft speech, he explains, appears in the Quran both as a command and in how prophets addressed even hostile people. It is not weakness or a lack of assertiveness; it is the caller's duty to remove obstacles, because harsh delivery forces listeners to fight their ego as well as the message and puts them on the defensive. He tells of a gentle teacher in his village whose talks on love only reached rough farmers once he spoke about hellfire, showing audiences differ, yet softness generally works, and guidance is Allah's gift, not a license to judge. Al-Khidr, after Musa broke his promise three times, parted from him gently and still explained everything, because he had been given mercy before knowledge; knowledge without mercy produces the destruction seen on today's screens. Ibrahim called his idol-worshipping father by a tender name, said he feared for him, and answered threats of stoning with peace and prayers for forgiveness, consistently. Young people should therefore never be harsh with parents, not even say 'uff', and should serve rather than correct them. Finally, Allah told Musa and Harun to speak gently to Pharaoh, the worst tyrant, so his ego would not block him. Masajid exist to serve and welcome people, and the only goal is hearts finding Allah.

outline.heading: Opening
Soft speech: command and prophetic example
outline.gist: Allah commands soft speech and the prophets used it with tyrants and enemies; it does not mean lacking assertiveness or letting people walk over you.

outline.heading: Do not give people two obstacles
outline.gist: Harsh speech makes people both accept the message and overcome their ego; whoever calls to Allah must lessen the obstacles between people and the truth.

outline.heading: The speaker does the most work
outline.gist: No one enjoys being lectured, so the speaker's job is to do as much work as possible so the listener does as little as possible.

outline.heading: Tone decides whether people get defensive
outline.gist: Beyond sound content and timing, tone matters: an aggressive delivery provokes pushback and justification, while a soft one leaves only the discomfort of being wrong. The scholars he learned from were all soft-spoken.

outline.heading: His gentle teacher in the village
outline.gist: A tender teacher's talks on love did not reach the rough farmers of his village; when he finally gave a khutbah on hellfire in 2003 the masjid overflowed the next morning, so audiences differ, though softness generally works.

outline.heading: Guidance is a gift, not a license to be harsh
outline.gist: We are guided only by Allah's generosity, so it is bad manners to judge or be harsh with those whose hearts have not yet opened; even in war the Quran says you were once lost too.

outline.heading: Musa learns someone knows more
outline.gist: After Musa told Bani Israel no one knew more than him, he learned of a more knowledgeable servant and set out to learn, because prophets seek knowledge wherever it is found.

outline.heading: 'You will not be able to bear with me'
outline.gist: The Quran calls him only a servant of Allah; he sees him as the decree of Allah in action, and he warns Musa that he will not understand his actions.

outline.heading: Musa insists on companionship
outline.gist: Musa wanted to accompany him, not just ask questions; the condition was not to ask until told. No ordinary human, sheikh or otherwise, may ask for such blind following.

outline.heading: The ship and the boy
outline.gist: Musa objected every time: when the servant holed a poor family's ship, and when he took a child's life, apologising after each protest.

outline.heading: Rebuilding a wall for a stingy village
outline.gist: The village refused them the customary hospitality, yet the servant rebuilt a collapsing wall, heavy labour, and Musa objected a third time.

outline.heading: 'This is the parting between us'
outline.gist: After Musa broke his word three times, the servant could have been harsh but simply and gently said they must part ways.

outline.heading: The explanations
outline.gist: The hole saved the ship from a king seizing sound vessels, the boy would have led good parents to disbelief, and the wall protected two orphans' treasure.

outline.heading: What Musa missed
outline.gist: Had he stayed silent he would have seen more of Allah's subtle work behind why one person thrives and another suffers; still, the servant took the time to explain.

outline.heading: Mercy before knowledge
outline.gist: Allah describes the servant as given mercy first and knowledge second, which is why he was gentle and patient; knowledge and technology without mercy produce bombing, genocide and poverty.

outline.heading: Watching the world burn on split screens
outline.gist: Past brutality was not broadcast; now we watch cities burning on divided screens and must find ways to cope with this needless show of dominance.

outline.heading: How Ibrahim spoke to his father
outline.gist: The passage is chosen for the way Ibrahim addressed his father.

outline.heading: 'Ya abati': the tender form
outline.gist: Changing a letter in Arabic makes a word more affectionate, as when the Prophet shortened Aisha's name; Ibrahim used the tender form of 'my father'.

outline.heading: Interlude
'Why worship what neither hears nor sees?'
outline.gist: Speaking to a leader of his people who was his father or uncle, Ibrahim gives the basic argument and says he is not better, only given knowledge his father had not received.

outline.heading: 'I fear for you'
outline.gist: He warns his father against serving Shaytan and says he fears the slightest touch of Allah's punishment reaching him.

outline.heading: Threatened with stoning, he answers with peace
outline.gist: His father threatens to stone him and drives him out; Ibrahim replies 'peace be upon you' and promises to seek his Lord's forgiveness for him.

outline.heading: Gentle toward a hostile father
outline.gist: Ibrahim was later told not to seek forgiveness for those hostile to the faith, but here, facing abuse and threats of violence, his speech stayed soft.

outline.heading: Most of you have parents who support your faith
outline.gist: Apart from some converts, the more religious you are the prouder your parents are; even parents who forbade Islam would still be owed soft speech.

outline.heading: Before you raise your voice at your parents
outline.gist: Ibrahim offered peace, prayer and to leave when asked; remember him before you yell at or point fingers at your mother or father.

outline.heading: Ibrahim was consistent
outline.gist: The point of the story is that his tone never changed: loving at the start and loving when threatened with death.

outline.heading: Not even 'uff': the weakest sound
outline.gist: If you are not facing what Ibrahim faced, why the anger? Of Arabic letters the fa has no feature of strength, and 'uff' is barely a word, yet even it is forbidden toward parents.

outline.heading: You are not here to correct your parents
outline.gist: Young people who catch parents in mistakes should not become self-righteous: even a prophet approached his father emotionally, not by saying 'you are wrong'. Your job is to serve them, change yourself, and be thankful.

outline.heading: Sent to the worst tyrant
outline.gist: Pharaoh enslaved a whole people, deemed them less human and declared himself the highest lord.

outline.heading: 'Speak to him gently'
outline.gist: One would expect a forceful approach backed by Allah's power, yet Musa and Harun were told to speak softly so he might remember or feel reverence.

outline.heading: Removing the ego obstacle, even for Pharaoh
outline.gist: Soft speech left Pharaoh only his own self-deception to deal with, bringing him a step closer to God; he still refused, but the caller's part is done.

outline.heading: Masajid are here to serve
outline.gist: Masajid are not countries and Muslim institutions are not governments; their only purpose is to serve and to make the way in easier, never intimidating.

outline.heading: Greet the newcomer
outline.gist: He prayed for nine years beside people whose names he never learned; at Wellness they arranged for people to greet anyone they see for the first time.

outline.heading: The goal is hearts finding Allah
outline.gist: If harshness was ever acceptable it was with Pharaoh, yet softness was commanded; we may be accountable for making it hard for people, and the only objective is drawing hearts to Allah.

24:30.ar: قُل لِّلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ يَغُضُّواْ مِنۡ أَبۡصَٰرِهِمۡ وَيَحۡفَظُواْ فُرُوجَهُمۡۚ ذَٰلِكَ أَزۡكَىٰ لَهُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ خَبِيرُۢ بِمَا يَصۡنَعُونَ
24:30.en: Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do

24:31.ar: وَقُل لِّلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتِ يَغۡضُضۡنَ مِنۡ أَبۡصَٰرِهِنَّ وَيَحۡفَظۡنَ فُرُوجَهُنَّ وَلَا يُبۡدِينَ زِينَتَهُنَّ إِلَّا مَا ظَهَرَ مِنۡهَاۖ وَلۡيَضۡرِبۡنَ بِخُمُرِهِنَّ عَلَىٰ جُيُوبِهِنَّۖ وَلَا يُبۡدِينَ زِينَتَهُنَّ إِلَّا لِبُعُولَتِهِنَّ أَوۡ ءَابَآئِهِنَّ أَوۡ ءَابَآءِ بُعُولَتِهِنَّ أَوۡ أَبۡنَآئِهِنَّ أَوۡ أَبۡنَآءِ بُعُولَتِهِنَّ أَوۡ إِخۡوَٰنِهِنَّ أَوۡ بَنِيٓ إِخۡوَٰنِهِنَّ أَوۡ بَنِيٓ أَخَوَٰتِهِنَّ أَوۡ نِسَآئِهِنَّ أَوۡ مَا مَلَكَتۡ أَيۡمَٰنُهُنَّ أَوِ ٱلتَّٰبِعِينَ غَيۡرِ أُوْلِي ٱلۡإِرۡبَةِ مِنَ ٱلرِّجَالِ أَوِ ٱلطِّفۡلِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَمۡ يَظۡهَرُواْ عَلَىٰ عَوۡرَٰتِ ٱلنِّسَآءِۖ وَلَا يَضۡرِبۡنَ بِأَرۡجُلِهِنَّ لِيُعۡلَمَ مَا يُخۡفِينَ مِن زِينَتِهِنَّۚ وَتُوبُوٓاْ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعًا أَيُّهَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تُفۡلِحُونَ
24:31.en: And tell the believing women to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts and not expose their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof and to wrap [a portion of] their headcovers over their chests and not expose their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, that which their right hands possess, or those male attendants having no physical desire, or children who are not yet aware of the private aspects of women. And let them not stamp their feet to make known what they conceal of their adornment. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you might succeed

2:273.ar: لِلۡفُقَرَآءِ ٱلَّذِينَ أُحۡصِرُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ لَا يَسۡتَطِيعُونَ ضَرۡبࣰ ا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ يَحۡسَبُهُمُ ٱلۡجَاهِلُ أَغۡنِيَآءَ مِنَ ٱلتَّعَفُّفِ تَعۡرِفُهُم بِسِيمَٰهُمۡ لَا يَسۡـَٔلُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ إِلۡحَافࣰ اۗ وَمَا تُنفِقُواْ مِنۡ خَيۡرࣲ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِهِۦ عَلِيمٌ
2:273.en: [Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all]. And whatever you spend of good - indeed, Allah is Knowing of it

24:33.ar: وَلۡيَسۡتَعۡفِفِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَجِدُونَ نِكَاحًا حَتَّىٰ يُغۡنِيَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضۡلِهِۦۗ وَٱلَّذِينَ يَبۡتَغُونَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ مِمَّا مَلَكَتۡ أَيۡمَٰنُكُمۡ فَكَاتِبُوهُمۡ إِنۡ عَلِمۡتُمۡ فِيهِمۡ خَيۡرࣰ اۖ وَءَاتُوهُم مِّن مَّالِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِيٓ ءَاتَىٰكُمۡۚ وَلَا تُكۡرِهُواْ فَتَيَٰتِكُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡبِغَآءِ إِنۡ أَرَدۡنَ تَحَصُّنࣰ ا لِّتَبۡتَغُواْ عَرَضَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۚ وَمَن يُكۡرِههُّنَّ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ إِكۡرَٰهِهِنَّ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
24:33.en: But let them who find not [the means for] marriage abstain [from sexual relations] until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those who seek a contract [for eventual emancipation] from among whom your right hands possess - then make a contract with them if you know there is within them goodness and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity, to seek [thereby] the temporary interests of worldly life. And if someone should compel them, then indeed, Allah is [to them], after their compulsion, Forgiving and Merciful

ElFKMWEm4io.speaker: adnan
ElFKMWEm4io.speaker_note: continues his own Ramadan values series with two values each morning
ElFKMWEm4io.title: The Values of Islam: Haya (Moral Awareness and Sensitivity) and 'Iffah (Restraint and Chastity)
ElFKMWEm4io.one_line: Haya is not shyness but moral awareness and sensitivity, the one value with no upper limit; 'iffah is the restraint that refuses to cheapen oneself.
ElFKMWEm4io.summary: The sheikh argues that translating haya as modesty or shyness shrinks it. It is moral awareness and sensitivity: knowing oneself and one's surroundings and responding to them. He gathers prophetic narrations: 'if you have no haya, do as you wish', haya brings only good, it is a branch of eman, and it is Islam's defining character. Linguistically haya comes from the root of life, so it is life at its height; the dead are defined by not responding, and the elderly lose filters as awareness fades. Unlike every other value, which turns harmful when pushed too far, haya has no limit, which is why the Prophet emphasised it so often and was more sensitive than a secluded maiden. Haya produces modest dress and lowered gaze for both men and women, without demanding weakness from strong, confident women, and its absence shows in people who barge in, block entrances or run stop signs. 'Iffah is not repression but restraint over how appetites for wealth, sex and power are pursued, the law that keeps desire's marketplace from swallowing the city, as advertising does today. It is the refusal to cheapen oneself, seen in the poor who never beg, the unmarried who stay chaste, and the opposite of the boss's flatterer. Dignity, he concludes, is not a value but the result of these two.

outline.heading: Haya cannot be translated
outline.gist: Rendering haya as modesty reduces the concept and drains its meaning.

outline.heading: Moral awareness and sensitivity
outline.gist: Haya is not toxic shame, guilt or humiliation but moral elegance: awareness of self and surroundings.

outline.heading: A teaching from early prophethood
outline.gist: If you have no haya, do as you wish: without it there is no restraint at all.

outline.heading: Haya brings only good
outline.gist: Said to a man rebuking his brother for it; haya is also a branch of eman.

outline.heading: Islam's defining character
outline.gist: Every religion has a defining trait and Islam's is haya; the slang sense of shyness causes confusion.

outline.heading: Shyness is a behaviour, haya a value
outline.gist: Depending on the situation haya may produce shyness or even loudness.

outline.heading: Haya as the height of life
outline.gist: The Arabic pattern makes haya the highest manifestation of hayat, life.

outline.heading: The dead do not respond
outline.gist: Death is a lack of response; the more aware a living being is, the more alive.

outline.heading: Losing filters with age
outline.gist: Elderly relatives who say anything show fading awareness; haya becomes consideration.

outline.heading: Every value is governed and limited
outline.gist: Truth, justice and moral absolutism rank the values, and moderation applies each one.

outline.heading: Too much of a value becomes a problem
outline.gist: Generosity, for example, can harm one's family when pushed too far.

outline.heading: The one value with no limit
outline.gist: The Prophet repeated haya so often because with it, the more the better.

outline.heading: More sensitive than a secluded maiden
outline.gist: Other values flip into their opposites; the Prophet's awareness was heightened all his life.

outline.heading: Why haya becomes modesty
outline.gist: Awareness of oneself and others translates into how one dresses and behaves, as with the Prophet's haya toward Uthman.

outline.heading: Men lowering the gaze
outline.gist: Aware of women around him, a man lowers his gaze literally and figuratively and dresses respectfully.

outline.heading: Strong women with haya
outline.gist: Haya does not mean weakness; aware women dress and carry themselves mindful of how society works.

outline.heading: People who barge in
outline.gist: Without awareness people are loud and clumsy; the aware person scans the room for what would bother others.

outline.heading: Big trucks and stop signs
outline.gist: Living as if no one else exists is not evil but a loss of moral awareness.

outline.heading: A society of considerate people
outline.gist: A masjid and society full of haya respects space and privacy and rises.

outline.heading: 'Iffah: the poor thought to be rich
outline.gist: Allah describes needy people whose restraint makes the unaware think them wealthy.

outline.heading: Restraint, not repression
outline.gist: Islam recognises appetites; 'iffah is the law that governs desire's marketplace.

outline.heading: When the marketplace swallows the city
outline.gist: Advertising during a football game sells everything with bodies because nothing restrains it.

outline.heading: Refusing to cheapen oneself
outline.gist: Haya and 'iffah together protect human dignity.

outline.heading: Losing dignity through carelessness
outline.gist: Running an intersection invites deserved insult; those unable to marry must keep chaste.

outline.heading: Zina sells the self cheaply
outline.gist: Falling into what Allah saw as beneath you sells your own dignity.

outline.heading: Restraint more valuable than wealth
outline.gist: The poor who refuse to beg keep their dignity; a Muslim sells himself for nothing.

outline.heading: The boss's pet
outline.gist: Flattering superiors for advancement sells dignity, and a person with haya will not accept it either.

outline.heading: Etiquette versus selling dignity
outline.gist: Good manners are different from trading dignity for sex, wealth or status.

outline.heading: Dignity is a result, not a value
outline.gist: Practise haya and 'iffah and dignity follows throughout life.

themes.label: Character and manners (akhlaq)
themes.note: Consideration for others in shared spaces, roads and masjids.

themes.label: Moderation and balance (wasatiyyah)
themes.note: Every value has a limit except haya.

themes.label: Modernity, secularism, materialism and their effects
themes.note: Advertising that sells everything through bodies.

themes.label: Self-value, self-worth, confidence
themes.note: Dignity as the fruit of refusing to sell oneself cheaply.
